title: Boxes in Boxes

post.author: u/lowmarsh_gate_jenifry
post.title: I'm the night gate clerk at a container yard. Tonight our record says a box left half an hour before it arrived, and the bill charges its owner for minus 30 minutes.

blocks.text: I'm Jenifry, night gate clerk at Lowmarsh Yard, where shipping containers wait between ships and lorries. Lorries come and go from 20:00 to 06:00, Monday to Friday nights; by day the cranes have the lanes.
The boxes are the whole trick: each is the same size, with the same corner fittings, so any ship, train or lorry carries it without knowing what's inside.

Two programs keep our record. When a box comes in, the gate system writes the time, on the gate server: the old computer in my office, set to UK time. When a box goes out, the departures service writes it; a service is a program running all night doing one job. Billing subtracts one from the other, charging storage by the minute.

Until Monday 9 February, departures ran on the gate server too. Then our contractor, Bleddyn, packed it into a box of its own. Software borrowed the shipping trick: pack a program with every file it needs into one standard box, and it runs the same on any machine. That box is called a container; Docker, a tool, packs and runs them.

Packing goes in steps. First you write a recipe. Docker builds it, line by line, into a sealed box called an image; each line adds a layer, a sheet of changes laid over the ones below. Then Docker starts a running copy of the image: the container.

The recipe is called a Dockerfile. Ours has three lines: the first names the base image, a small ready-made set of system files to build on; the second copies our program in; the third says what to start.

Bleddyn chose a slim base to keep the box small. It holds no time-zone data: the rule book listing time zones, the regions that keep one clock, and when each moves its clocks. With no rule book, our program writes UTC, the world's reference clock.

The machine a container runs on is called its host. Ours is a rented server, set to UTC. Settings reach a container in two steps: you hand them over when it starts, as environment variables, like labels stuck on the box; then the program reads them. We handed over none.

All winter it didn't matter: UK winter time is UTC. The clocks went forward at 01:00 on Sunday 29 March, and we close from Saturday 06:00 to Monday 20:00, so tonight, Monday 30 March, was the first shift since. UK time is now UTC plus one hour; that gap between a place's clock and UTC is called its offset.
Ten boxes came and went tonight. At 23:20 a lorry dropped QZRU 2051144. Each gate log line shows the date, the time by the gate server's clock, IN, and the box number.
At 23:50 I watched another lorry take it out. The departures log has the same columns:
By our record, it left half an hour before it arrived.

blocks.label: qzru_2051144_record.png

diagram.aria: Monday 30 March 2026, 22:30 to midnight, UK time. Real stay of box QZRU 2051144: 23:20 to 23:50, 30 minutes. The record: OUT logged at 22:50, IN logged at 23:20, so the record runs backwards from 22:50 to 23:20, minus 30 minutes.

blocks.caption: Redrawn from the two logs. The box was in the yard from 23:20 to 23:50 by the clock on my wall. The gate log wrote 23:20 in UK time; the departures log wrote 22:50, the same moment in UTC. Billing took one from the other: minus 30 minutes.

blocks.text: Billing charged its owner for minus 30 minutes, and every other box tonight an hour short. On Monday 16 March, a winter night, every bill was right.
Bleddyn says nothing is broken: each program wrote the true time by its own clock. What should we change?

comments.author: u/grey_pager
comments.text: Two honest lines and an impossible record. Look inside the box, not at it. What does a container carry from its image, and what does it borrow from the machine it lands on? Those labels stuck on your box are environment variables, and the one that names a time zone is TZ, as in TZ=Europe/London; you passed none. Now ask: which clock did each line use? What did the two logs say on 16 March, and would anyone have seen the difference then? And what does billing know about either time when it takes one from the other?

replies.author: u/lowmarsh_gate_jenifry
replies.text: Gate: UK time. Departures: UTC. On 16 March they read the same, because UK winter time is UTC, so nobody could have seen it. Billing gets two bare times and subtracts them.

comments.author: u/one_clock_lancelyn
comments.text: Containers use the host's clock. A container isn't a separate computer; it's just programs running on the host, and there is one clock in that machine. Your host is set to UTC and your container writes UTC: there's your cause. Set the host's time zone to UK time and the container follows. Five minutes, no rebuild.

comments.author: u/switch_it_off_hywel
comments.text: Has anyone restarted departures since Sunday? A restart means stopping a program and starting it again. Plenty of programs read the time-zone setting once, when they start, and keep it in memory. Yours has been running since before the clocks went forward. It may still think it's winter.

comments.author: u/lowmarsh_contractor_bleddyn
comments.text: Bleddyn here. The gate server is out of support, meaning its maker no longer sends fixes, and it gets switched off at the end of June; that's why departures moved first. If you want, I can put departures back on it tonight. On that machine both programs read the same UK clock, the way they did all winter.

reply.prompt: The gate opens again at 20:00 on Tuesday. What should Lowmarsh change? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Set the host machine's time zone to UK time, so the container picks up the right hour.
options.verdict: The host's setting stays outside the box
options.part2: Bleddyn set the host to UK time on Tuesday afternoon. In the sim I did the same and replayed tonight: QZRU 2051144 still left at 22:50 by the departures log, billed -30 minutes, and the ten boxes came out 690 minutes billed against 1,290 real, 600 short. The container was started from the image, and the image's files say nothing about the UK; the host's setting never crossed into the box. Lancelyn was half right: on most systems a container does share the host's count of seconds, but it reads what those seconds mean from files inside its own image. Tuesday night every box was billed an hour short again.
options.senior: A container brings its own system files: its time-zone data, its libraries, its settings files, all from the image. It shares the host's machine but not the host's configuration. That is the point of containers, the reason the same image behaves the same on a laptop and a rented server, and it means the host is the wrong place to fix a container. Configuration reaches a container from outside only when you pass it in, as environment variables or mounted files, and even then the image must hold the data the setting points to.

options.text: Write every time with its offset from UTC, in both the gate and departures systems.
options.part2: Bleddyn changed both programs to write the offset after every time. The gate log now reads 2026-03-30 23:20+01:00 and departures 2026-03-30 22:50+00:00, and billing turns both into UTC before it takes one from the other. In the sim, with offsets on, QZRU 2051144 bills 30 minutes and the night 1,290 minutes, right to the minute; on 16 March the same; and the answer holds whatever base image, TZ or host departures uses, even on the old gate server. We re-billed the ten boxes by hand. When the gate server was switched off at the end of June, the gate system moved into a container on the same slim base and wrote its times with +00:00; billing never noticed.
options.senior: A bare clock reading is half a fact: 23:20 means nothing until you know which clock read it. Write every time with its offset from UTC, or in UTC with a Z, and convert to one clock before comparing or subtracting. Then it no longer matters which machine, image or time zone wrote the time, and winter can't hide a difference that summer exposes. Show local time to people at the last moment, from proper time-zone data, but store and compare times that carry their offset.

options.text: Restart the departures container tonight, so it reads the new clock time on starting.
options.verdict: A fresh copy of the same box
options.part2: Bleddyn restarted departures at 01:00 on Tuesday night. In the sim I did the same, mid-night: the log says the container restarted from the same image, with the same files, and still writes UTC. On Tuesday night the boxes that left after 01:00 were billed an hour short like the rest. Hywel's rule is true of some programs, but this one never had a rule book to read: restarting a container starts a fresh copy of the same sealed image.
options.senior: A container is a running copy of an image, and an image does not change once built. Restarting throws away the running copy and starts another from the same image, with the same files and the same missing data, so it fixes only problems that live in the running copy's memory. Before reaching for a restart, ask whether the fault is in the copy or in the box it was copied from.

options.text: Move departures back to the old gate server it ran on before February, where times agreed.
options.part2: Bleddyn moved departures back onto the gate server on Tuesday. In the sim, with departures on the old server, all ten boxes bill right: 1,290 minutes, because both programs read the same UK clock. It stayed right all spring. At the end of June the gate server was switched off as planned, departures went back into its container from the same image, and the first night's bills were an hour short again: still no offset on any line, and by then nobody remembered why.
options.senior: Moving back works because both programs then share one clock, but it hides the fault instead of fixing it: two programs subtracting bare times only agree while they happen to run on the same setting. It also undoes the move to containers and ties departures to a machine that is about to be switched off. Fix the record, not the location: once every time carries its offset, any program can run anywhere.

sim.title: Replay the night at Lowmarsh Yard
sim.lede: You're Jenifry at 20:00 on Monday 30 March 2026, the first night shift since the clocks went forward, so UK time is UTC plus one hour. Ten boxes come and go tonight, each dropped off by one lorry and collected by another. The gate system logs each arrival on the gate server in UK time; the departures service logs each departure from its container. Billing takes one time from the other. Pick the night (this one, or Monday 16 March, a winter night, with the same ten moves), the departures base image (slim, or slim plus a layer of time-zone data), the TZ environment variable, the host's time zone, where departures runs (its container, or the old gate server), and whether every time carries its offset. Restart the container whenever you like. Then play the night one event at a time, or to 06:00.
sim.tryThis: Try this: press Next event ten times. At 23:50 QZRU 2051144 leaves, logged 22:50, billed -30 minutes. Run the night: 1,290 real minutes, 690 billed, 600 short. Switch to 16 March: every bill right. Back on 30 March, set the host to UK time, or restart the container mid-night: nothing changes. Set TZ to Europe/London on the slim image: still UTC. Add the time-zone data layer as well: UK time. Put departures back on the old gate server: right tonight. Turn offsets on: right on both nights, whatever else you pick.

explain.oneLine: Nothing broke. The departures container was built from a slim image with no time-zone data, so it wrote UTC; the gate server wrote UK time. All winter the two read the same. On the first night after the clocks went forward, billing subtracted 23:20 in UK time from 22:50 in UTC and got minus 30 minutes.

steps.title: An image is the sealed box; a container is one running copy.
steps.text: Docker works in steps. First, a Dockerfile lists what goes in: a base image to start from, then the program, then the command to start it. Second, Docker builds the image, adding one layer for each step, each a sheet of file changes laid over the ones below. Third, the image is sealed: Docker's documentation says an image cannot be changed once it is created, only replaced by a new one. Fourth, Docker starts a container, a running copy of the image; one image can start many. What can go wrong at the first step is what you leave out. Gatebase:slim left out the time-zone data.

steps.title: The time zone lived inside the box.
steps.text: When a program asks for the time in a given place, the system answers in steps. It reads the clock's count of seconds, which on most systems is kept in UTC. It looks up which time zone to use. It opens the time-zone data, the rule book usually built from the IANA Time Zone Database, to find that zone's offset on that date. Then it adds the offset. In the departures container no zone was named and no rule book was there, so the answer stayed in UTC. The gate server has both, so it wrote UK time.

steps.title: The host's settings stay outside.
steps.text: A container runs on its host's machine, but it reads its files from its own image, not from the host. That is what makes it portable: the same image behaves the same on Bleddyn's laptop and on the rented server. Settings get in only when you pass them in, usually as environment variables when the container starts, such as TZ=Europe/London. Even then, the image must hold the data the setting names. TZ on the slim image still gives UTC, on most systems without any error; TZ plus a layer of time-zone data gives UK time.

steps.title: Two honest clocks, one subtraction.
steps.text: The gate log wrote 2026-03-30 23:20 and the departures log 2026-03-30 22:50. Each was true by its own clock, but neither said which clock. Billing took one bare time from the other. In winter the UK's offset is zero, so UK time and UTC read the same and every bill was right; that is why February and the first half of March looked fine. After the clocks went forward, every departure read an hour early: QZRU 2051144's 30 minutes became minus 30, and the night's 1,290 minutes were billed as 690.

steps.title: Why the other fixes miss.
steps.text: Setting the host to UK time changes a file the container never reads. Restarting starts a fresh copy of the same image, with the same missing data. Moving departures back to the gate server works only because both programs then share one clock; it lasts until the server is switched off in June, and the bare times are still there. Even TZ with a time-zone layer only puts both programs on one local clock again, and two times that don't say their offset can still be misread by the next program. Writing the offset with every time fixes the record itself.

diagram.aria: The fix, drawn for tomorrow night. The gate server, set to UK time, writes arrivals with their offset: 23:20+01:00. The departures container, started from gatebase:slim on a host set to UTC, writes departures with their offset: 22:50+00:00. Billing converts both to UTC before subtracting, and gets 30 minutes in any season.

explain.caption: The fix, drawn for tomorrow night. Each program writes its time with its offset from UTC: the gate server 23:20+01:00, the departures container 22:50+00:00. Billing turns both into UTC before subtracting. The host's setting no longer matters, and in the sim the night bills 1,290 minutes on 30 March and on 16 March.

fix.title: The fix: every time carries its offset
fix.text: Change both programs to write each time with its offset from UTC, in the international date format, ISO 8601: the gate system 2026-03-30 23:20+01:00, departures 2026-03-30 22:50+00:00. Change billing to turn both into UTC before it subtracts. Then it doesn't matter which clock each program reads, which image departures was built from, or what the host is set to. Check it in the sim: offsets on, 30 March and 16 March both bill 1,290 minutes, and QZRU 2051144 bills 30. Re-bill tonight's ten boxes by hand. If people at the gate want to see UK time on a screen, convert at the screen, from an image that carries time-zone data.

limits: Offsets fix new lines only. Every departure logged since 29 March without one must be read as UTC and every arrival as UK time, by hand or with a one-off script, before the old bills are corrected.

An offset says what the clock read, not what it will read. To plan a future time in UK time, such as a collection booked for next winter, store the time zone's name too, and keep the time-zone data in the image up to date.
Any program that still subtracts bare times, or a new container on the slim image that shows times to people, will repeat tonight. Check every reader of these logs, not just billing.

explain.seniorTake: Containers give you one sealed box that behaves the same everywhere, and the price is that everything the program depends on must be inside the box or passed in at the door. An image is built in layers from a base image and never changes once built; a container is one running copy of it; configuration comes in from outside, usually as environment variables, and the host's own settings stay outside. So when a containerised program behaves differently from the old one, look first at what the image left out: time-zone data, certificates, fonts, locale files are common gaps in slim images. The deeper lesson is about data that crosses programs. A time without its offset is only true on the machine that wrote it. Store and send times in UTC or with their offset, compare only after converting, and turn them into local time at the last step, for people. Do that and a winter that hides a difference can't trick you in spring.

realWorld.title: Docker documentation: what an image is
realWorld.text: Docker's guide says "A container image is a standardized package that includes all of the files, binaries, libraries, and configurations to run a container." It adds that "Images are immutable. Once an image is created, it can't be modified. You can only make a new image or add changes on top of it", and that "Container images are composed of layers."

realWorld.title: Docker documentation: what a container is
realWorld.text: "Simply put, containers are isolated processes for each of your app's components." And: "Each container has everything it needs to function with no reliance on any pre-installed dependencies on the host machine." That is why the host's time-zone setting did not reach the departures container.

realWorld.title: Dockerfile reference: FROM, COPY, CMD and ENV
realWorld.text: The reference lists FROM as "Create a new build stage from a base image", COPY as "Copy files and directories" and CMD as "Specify default commands". On settings: "The environment variables set using ENV will persist when a container is run from the resulting image", and you can "change them using docker run --env <key>=<value>".

realWorld.title: The IANA Time Zone Database
realWorld.text: The rule book behind most systems' time-zone data is the IANA Time Zone Database, often called tz or zoneinfo. A slim image that leaves those files out has nothing to look a zone up in.

realWorld.title: GOV.UK: when the clocks change
realWorld.text: "In the UK the clocks go forward 1 hour at 1am on the last Sunday in March, and back 1 hour at 2am on the last Sunday in October." In 2026 that is 29 March and 25 October. Between those dates UK time is British Summer Time, UTC plus one hour; the rest of the year it is Greenwich Mean Time, the same as UTC.

asked: Image or container: what is the difference?
How do you pass configuration into a container?
How should a system store times?
interview.answer: An image is the packaged, read-only template: a base image plus layers, one for each step of the Dockerfile, holding the program and every file it needs. It never changes once built; you build a new one. A container is a running copy of an image, with its own small writable layer on top that is thrown away when the container is removed, and one image can start many containers. Configuration should come from outside the image, so the same image runs in test and production: usually environment variables passed when the container starts, such as docker run --env, or files mounted in, with secrets handled by the platform's secret store rather than baked into the image. The host's own settings do not leak in; a container reads its own files. For times, store and send them in UTC or with their offset from UTC, in a standard format such as 2026-03-30T22:50:00Z or 23:20+01:00, compare only after converting to one clock, and convert to local time at the last step for a person, using up-to-date time-zone data; keep the zone's name as well when you plan future local times. A story I'd tell: a container yard moved its departures service into a container built on a slim image with no time-zone data, so it wrote UTC while the gate server wrote UK time. All winter they matched. On the first night after the clocks went forward, a box that stayed 30 minutes was billed minus 30, and the night's 1,290 minutes were billed as 690. Setting the host's time zone and restarting changed nothing; writing the offset with every time fixed it in every season.

terms.def: The container yard in this story. Lorries drop off and collect boxes from 20:00 to 06:00, Monday to Friday nights; by day the lanes belong to the cranes.
The person at the yard's gate overnight who checks each lorry and box in and out. Jenifry is Lowmarsh's.
A steel box of standard size and corner fittings, so any ship, train, lorry or crane can move it without knowing what is inside. The comparison this case is built on.
The number painted on every shipping container: four letters for the owner, then seven digits. QZRU 2051144 is the box in this story.
The program that writes down the time each box arrives at Lowmarsh. It runs on the gate server, in UK time.
The old computer in the gate office, set to UK time. Out of support and due to be switched off at the end of June.
A program that runs all the time and does one job for other things, like the departures service, which writes down when each box leaves.
The program that writes down the time each box leaves Lowmarsh. It ran on the gate server until 9 February 2026, then in a container.
The program that takes each box's arrival time from its departure time and charges storage by the minute.
An outside person or firm hired to do a job. Bleddyn looks after Lowmarsh's computers and moved departures into a container.
A running copy of an image: a program packed with every file it needs, kept apart from other programs on the same machine. Like a shipping box, it runs the same on any host.
The most widely used tool for building images and running containers from them.
The sealed box a container is started from: a base image plus layers holding the program and its files. It never changes once built; you build a new one instead.
One sheet of file changes in an image, added by one step of the Dockerfile and laid over the layers below. Docker says images are made of layers.
The recipe for an image: a text file of steps that Docker builds in order. Lowmarsh's has three lines: FROM, COPY and CMD.
Three Dockerfile steps: FROM names the base image to build on, COPY puts files into the image, and CMD says which program to start when a container runs.
The ready-made image a Dockerfile starts from: a small set of system files to build on. Everything the program needs that it lacks must be added.
A base image cut down to keep it small and quick to move. What is cut, such as time-zone data, is missing in every container started from it.
The slim base image departures is built on in this story. It holds no time-zone data, so programs in it write UTC.
A region that keeps the same clock time, such as the UK, written Europe/London in time-zone data.
The rule book a system reads to turn UTC into local time: each zone's offset and the dates its clocks change. Usually built from the IANA Time Zone Database.
The shared record of local time rules for places worldwide, often called tz or zoneinfo, kept by IANA. Most systems' time-zone data comes from it.
Short for Coordinated Universal Time, the world's reference clock. It never moves for summer, so times from anywhere can be compared on it.
Greenwich Mean Time in winter, the same as UTC; British Summer Time, UTC plus one hour, from the last Sunday in March to the last Sunday in October.
In the UK, at 01:00 on the last Sunday of March the clocks move to 02:00. In 2026 that was Sunday 29 March.
The gap between a place's clock and UTC at a moment, such as +01:00 for UK summer time and +00:00 in winter. Written after a time, it says which clock read it.
The machine a container runs on. Lowmarsh's is a rented server set to UTC. A container shares the machine but reads its own files, not the host's settings.
A named setting handed to a program when it starts, like a label stuck on the box. Docker passes them with ENV in the Dockerfile or docker run --env.
The environment variable that names a time zone, such as TZ=Europe/London. It works only if the image holds time-zone data for that zone.
Stopping a program and starting it again. For a container, a fresh running copy of the same image.
No longer receiving fixes from its maker, including security fixes. The usual reason to move a program off an old machine.
A date and clock reading with no offset, such as 2026-03-30 22:50. It is only true on the clock that wrote it.
The international standard for writing dates and times, such as 2026-03-30T23:20+01:00 or 2026-03-30T22:50Z, where Z means UTC.
The records that show who did what and when, kept so it can be checked later. Its times are only useful if they can be compared.
An international standard for running information security. Its Annex A lists controls, among them A.8.17 on clock synchronisation.
The control on clock synchronisation: keeping the clocks of information systems accurate and in step, so logs and records can be relied on.

atWork: Look for places where a program moved into a container and another program reads what it writes. It is a common pattern for a service moved into a slim container to start writing times in UTC beside an older one that writes local time, and for nobody to notice until the clocks change. Check three things. Does every time your systems store or send carry its offset, or is it in UTC with a Z? Do the programs that compare or subtract times convert them to one clock first? And what has your base image left out: time-zone data, certificates, locale files? Run a container from your image and ask it the time in your zone. If you deploy with containers on AWS, for example on ECS, the same rule holds: pass settings in as environment variables, and make sure the image holds the data they name. Standards: if your company is pursuing ISO/IEC 27001:2022, control A.8.17 asks for accurate, synchronised clocks on information systems, because audit trails depend on times that can be compared; times written without their offset by two systems make the comparison wrong even when both clocks are accurate. Decide the time format now, so the evidence is consistent before an auditor asks.

recall.prompt: Your team moved its order-reports service into a container in January. Tonight, the first night of summer time, the reports say dozens of orders were shipped an hour before they were packed. Packing times come from an old server set to local time. The container's image is a cut-down one, and nobody passed it any settings. What happened, and what would you change?

keyIdeas.idea: The image has no time-zone data, so the container writes UTC while the old server writes local time
The two bare times were compared without knowing which clock each used; in winter the offset was zero, so it was hidden
Write every time with its offset, or in UTC, and convert to one clock before comparing

recall.model: The container's cut-down image holds no time-zone data, so the program inside falls back to UTC, while the old server writes local time. Neither line says which clock it used, so the report compared two bare times. In winter the offset was zero, so local time and UTC read the same and nothing showed; tonight local time is UTC plus one and every shipping time reads an hour early. Changing the host or restarting won't help, since the container reads its own image. Write every time with its offset, such as +01:00, or in UTC with a Z, in both systems, and convert to UTC before comparing. Correct the old lines once.

recall.prompt: What is the difference between an image and a container?
options: An image is a running program; a container is the file it was saved to
An image is the sealed, unchanging package; a container is one running copy started from it
They are two names for the same thing
An image runs on the host; a container runs inside another container
recall.why: The image is built once, in layers, and does not change; a container is a running copy started from it, and one image can start many. Restarting a container starts a fresh copy of the same image.

recall.prompt: The departures container was built on a slim image with no time-zone data. Which change makes it write UK time?
options: Set the host machine's time zone to UK time
Pass TZ=Europe/London as an environment variable, and add time-zone data to the image
Pass TZ=Europe/London as an environment variable, and nothing else
recall.why: A container reads its own files, not the host's settings, and a restart starts the same image again. TZ names the zone, but the program can only look it up if the image holds time-zone data; without it, it stays in UTC.

recall.prompt: A gate log line reads 2026-03-30 23:20+01:00. What is that moment in UTC?
recall.why: +01:00 means the clock that wrote it was one hour ahead of UTC, so take the hour off: 22:20 UTC. That is how billing turns both logs into one clock before subtracting.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 5 months later. Every line has carried its offset since 31 March, and no bill has gone wrong. At the end of June the gate server was switched off and the gate system moved into a container on the same gatebase:slim image. In August Bleddyn added a screen in the gate hut that shows clerks each box's arrival in UK time. He started its container with TZ=Europe/London as an environment variable. The screen shows a 23:20 arrival as 22:20. On his laptop, built from a different base image, the same setting shows 23:20.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Why does the screen ignore the TZ setting, and how should Bleddyn fix it?

keyIdeas.idea: The image holds no time-zone data, so the program cannot look up the zone and falls back to UTC
A container reads the files in its own image, not those of the laptop or the host
Add the time-zone data as a layer and rebuild the image, keeping the stored times with offsets

coldCase.model: TZ only names a zone; the program still has to look Europe/London up in time-zone data, and gatebase:slim has no time-zone data. With no rule book it can't look up the zone, so it falls back to UTC, quietly, and shows 22:20. The container reads its own image's files, not the laptop's or the host's, which is why the same setting worked on the laptop's base image. Add the time-zone data to the image as a new layer in the Dockerfile and rebuild, keep passing TZ, and check it by asking a running container for the time. Keep the stored times with their offsets; convert to UK time only for the screen.
